title: What is a lakehouse in Microsoft Fabric?

claims.text: A Fabric lakehouse merges data-lake scale storage with warehouse-style querying: structured and unstructured data live in one location and can be analyzed with both Apache Spark and T-SQL, with no data movement between systems.
All managed lakehouse tables use the Delta Lake storage format, which supplies ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel over the underlying Parquet files.
A lakehouse splits its storage into two top-level areas: a managed Tables area reserved for Delta tables and a Files area for unstructured or non-Delta data.

When data lands in the managed Tables area, Fabric automatically validates the format (Delta only at present), extracts column names, types, compression, and partitioning metadata, and registers the table in the metastore so it is immediately queryable from Spark SQL or T-SQL without a manual CREATE TABLE.

Lakehouse and warehouse in Fabric share the same SQL engine and both persist data as Delta on OneLake; the practical decision points are tooling and workload: lakehouse is Spark-first and handles unstructured data, while the warehouse is T-SQL-first and supports multi-table transactions, which the lakehouse does not.

A proven pattern is to combine both item types in one workspace: land and transform raw data in a lakehouse with Spark (e.g., a medallion architecture), then surface curated datasets through a warehouse for SQL-centric reporting teams.

Data can enter a lakehouse through several routes: Spark notebooks, pipeline copy activities, Spark job definitions for compiled production ETL, Dataflows Gen2 for low-code preparation, or OneLake shortcuts that reference external data in place.

OneLake shortcuts give a lakehouse live, read-only references to data held elsewhere in OneLake, in external systems, or even in other tenants via cross-tenant data sharing, avoiding duplication of the underlying data.

Creating a lakehouse automatically provisions a companion SQL analytics endpoint, a read-only T-SQL surface intended for exploration, reporting, and ad-hoc queries rather than the full warehouse T-SQL feature set.

Only Delta tables surface through the lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint, including Delta tables reached via OneLake shortcuts; Parquet, CSV, and other formats must first be converted to Delta to be queryable there.

Since September 5, 2025, Fabric no longer auto-creates a default semantic model when a lakehouse is created, and previously existing default semantic models were decoupled from their parent items into independent semantic models by November 30, 2025.

From the lakehouse ribbon, an 'Analyze data with' dropdown opens the same data in different engines: the SQL analytics endpoint for T-SQL, an Eventhouse endpoint for KQL real-time analytics, or a new/existing Spark notebook.
